strand_c.title: Commission welcomes political agreement on the Programme for agile and rapid defence innovation (AGILE)
strand_c.authors: Directorate-General for Defence Industry and Space
strand_c.source: European Commission — Defence Industry and Space
strand_c.summary: This is a political agreement between the European Parliament and the Council, reached on 15 July 2026, and not yet final adopted legislation. The Commission proposed AGILE in March 2026 with a budget of €115 million, directed at small and medium-sized enterprises, start-ups and scale-ups rather than established defence primes. Work is to be organised around mission-driven challenges defined with member states, with the stated ambition of developing, testing and deploying products in weeks or months instead of years. The instrument is expected to be operational from 1 January 2027, with continuity intended through the proposed European Competitiveness Fund. The delivery timescales described are programme objectives, not demonstrated performance.

strand_c.reader_what: An expert report finds open access progress real but fragmented across member states, with rising publishing charges a structural barrier.
strand_c.reader_why: Fragmented national rules and costs shape what European research is actually readable.
strand_c.reader_more: The European Commission published an independent expert report reviewing open access across all 27 member states and eight non-EU countries. It finds genuine progress but persistent fragmentation: countries differ on legal enforceability, embargo periods, copyright mechanisms, repository requirements and monitoring. The report identifies what works, namely combining legislation, funder mandates and institutional support rather than relying on a single instrument, and notes that mandates tied to research assessment change behaviour while policies without operational support often do not. Rising article processing charges are flagged as a structural barrier that falls hardest on under-resourced institutions, with a call for systematic tracking of that spending.

strand_c.reader_why: Delay compresses the trilogue window and threatens a 2028 start for the next framework programme.
strand_c.reader_more: Legislative work on the next Horizon Europe and the European Competitiveness Fund has stalled while the European Parliament's budgets committee settles the Performance Framework Regulation, a horizontal set of monitoring rules from the Commission's July 2025 MFF proposal. The disagreement is between the S&D, which wants the regulation applied across all sectoral programmes at once, and the EPP, which opposes that. Committee votes originally set for 10 September were postponed and the plenary vote moved from 5 October to mid-November. Research Commissioner Ekaterina Zaharieva had said a deal by end-2026 was needed for a 1 January 2028 start. A separate dispute over expert councils governing Pillar 2 also remains open.

strand_c.reader_title: Finland's LUMI AI Factory to host a staged IQM quantum computer built for logical qubits
strand_c.reader_what: CSC will host LUMI-IQ, an IQM superconducting machine delivered in stages from 2027 to 2029.
strand_c.reader_why: Places error-corrected quantum hardware inside a European HPC and AI facility the host institution controls.
strand_c.reader_more: CSC - IT Center for Science in Kajaani will host LUMI-IQ, described as Europe's first superconducting quantum computer designed from the outset to operate with logical qubits. Logical qubits combine several error-prone physical qubits into a more reliable computational unit through quantum error correction. An IQM Halocene H4 system with 150 physical qubits arrives in 2027, with error-correction upgrades in 2028 and a Halocene H5 upgrade in 2029, jointly funded by the EuroHPC Joint Undertaking with Finland, Czechia, Norway and Poland. The machine will be integrated with the LUMI AI Factory's classical HPC and AI resources for hybrid workflows. Nothing has been delivered yet, so the announcement sets out a procurement and a schedule rather than an installed capability.

strand_c.reader_more: The European Commission published the European Innovation Act, aimed at closing the gap between Europe's research output and marketable products. The JRC used RHOMOLO, its regional economic model. Under a more conservative scenario the projected gain falls to almost EUR 256 billion.

strand_c.reader_more: Professor Walter Van Dyck of Vlerick Business School argues Belgium does not underspend on medicines relative to neighbours but spends badly, cutting prices hard to stay within budget and paying later in lost innovation. With researcher Paola Argiolas he sets out four proposals in a new policy paper supported by Novartis: reform the clawback, widen the price gap on off-patent medicines and ring-fence savings, pay for new medicines from day one and settle price later, and build a European fund for the most expensive advanced therapies.

strategic_pathways.reader_title: New MSCA pilot funds longer-term postdoctoral posts to counter research precarity
strategic_pathways.reader_what: A 22.5 million euro MSCA pilot selects institutions partly on the long-term job security they offer researchers.
strategic_pathways.reader_why: Ties EU research funding to employment conditions rather than project output alone.
strategic_pathways.reader_more: Choose Europe for Science is an MSCA pilot action aimed at making European research careers more attractive by tackling precarity and turning brain drain into brain gain. Academic and non-academic organisations recruit postdoctoral researchers with a view to employment beyond the project period, and its stated novelty is that applicants are assessed partly on the longer-term professional prospects they offer. A single legal entity in a Member State or Horizon Europe associated country applies, with associated partners possible. The call budget is 22.5 million euros, capped at 3.5 million per beneficiary, and projects should recruit at least three researchers for up to five years, with MSCA covering the first two to three. Full conditions sit in the 2025 MSCA Work Programme.

dynamic_shocks.title: A security reclassification abruptly narrows access to Europe’s research infrastructures
dynamic_shocks.plainly: Europe relies on research infrastructures. Separate primary evidence shows that a sudden security reclassification can change access quickly. Recent weak signals and historical material may strengthen the context, but neither can establish the shock on its own.
dynamic_shocks.second_order: Projects may keep their grants and institutions but still lose time, access or usable capacity while a replacement is found.
dynamic_shocks.why_easy_to_miss: The hypothesis appears when durable European capability evidence and a separately evidenced external pressure are read as one chain; low-weight current signals and history are then used only as context.
reasoning: Primary retained evidence shows European reliance on or expansion of research infrastructures.
Separate primary retained evidence shows a live mechanism for a sudden security reclassification.
Primary evidence contains 2 direct capability × pressure coupling record(s).
3 recent weak-signal item(s) point in the same direction; each is capped at 30% of a primary evidence item and none satisfies a primary threshold.
2 historical Strand-A item(s) provide structural context; they cannot serve as the current trigger.
The scenario becomes a shock only if the response is slower than the disruption.
conditions: Europe materially depends on research infrastructures for current or planned work.
A sudden security reclassification reaches the supplier, service, partner or rule that the European capability depends on.
Europe cannot substitute, reroute or absorb the change before projects begin losing usable capacity.
case_against: Recent media/weak-signal corroboration is intentionally down-weighted and cannot substitute for primary evidence.
The scenario still depends on the disruption arriving faster than Europe can respond.
prevention_actions: Maintain alternative facilities and access routes for projects that depend on shared infrastructure.
Avoid a single access system becoming the only route into several European facilities.
Use common, targeted screening rules rather than broad restrictions that fragment European access.
watch_for: Research previously treated as open is moved into a more restricted security category.
Different European countries apply materially different access decisions to the same work.
dynamic_shocks.net_assessment: Well supported enough to watch closely, with contextual signals reinforcing rather than carrying the case.

dynamic_shocks.title: A conflict escalation severs Europe’s access to open science and research data
dynamic_shocks.plainly: Europe relies on open science and research data. Separate primary evidence shows that an armed-conflict escalation can change access quickly. Recent weak signals and historical material may strengthen the context, but neither can establish the shock on its own.
dynamic_shocks.second_order: Projects may keep their grants and institutions but still lose time, access or usable capacity while a replacement is found.
dynamic_shocks.why_easy_to_miss: The hypothesis appears when durable European capability evidence and a separately evidenced external pressure are read as one chain; low-weight current signals and history are then used only as context.
reasoning: Primary retained evidence shows European reliance on or expansion of open science and research data.
Separate primary retained evidence shows a live mechanism for an armed-conflict escalation.
Primary evidence contains 1 direct capability × pressure coupling record(s).
2 recent weak-signal item(s) point in the same direction; each is capped at 30% of a primary evidence item and none satisfies a primary threshold.
2 historical Strand-A item(s) provide structural context; they cannot serve as the current trigger.
The scenario becomes a shock only if the response is slower than the disruption.
conditions: Europe materially depends on open science and research data for current or planned work.
An armed-conflict escalation reaches the supplier, service, partner or rule that the European capability depends on.
Europe cannot substitute, reroute or absorb the change before projects begin losing usable capacity.
case_against: Only one primary retained record currently links the European capability directly to the outside pressure.
The primary direct connection is concentrated in one source, so independent confirmation is still weak.
The primary corpus contains 5 strong sign(s) of substitution, resilience or policy response that could absorb the shock.
Recent media/weak-signal corroboration is intentionally down-weighted and cannot substitute for primary evidence.
The scenario still depends on the disruption arriving faster than Europe can respond.
prevention_actions: Separate genuinely sensitive research from ordinary open research instead of using blanket restrictions.
Use common European safeguards so institutions do not create incompatible access rules.
Prepare relocation, remote-access and project-transfer plans before a research corridor closes.
watch_for: A research corridor closes, staff are evacuated, or facilities become inaccessible.
European partners take over work that can no longer be carried out locally.
dynamic_shocks.net_assessment: Plausible, but important parts of the primary trigger or connection still need confirmation.

page_guarantee.rule: New records update candidate reasoning; the shelf is re-decided each scan from recomputed maturity. No record takes a slot automatically.
page_guarantee.creative_reserve: Reserve = grounded runners-up + a creative reserve of relevant, uncontradicted hypotheses (distant, cross-domain, emerging, weak-signal or partially grounded), at least 18 and topped up toward 45, rotated across wow levels with weight on surprise. They mature into page competition when grounded.

high_order_inference.publication_policy: Stage 7 claim-native selection treats the reasoning layer as a future-hypothesis corpus. Candidate formation is broad; missing roles, thin evidence and unrun counter-evidence tests lower maturity rather than forbidding the hypothesis. Grounded candidates compete only within their wow 1-5 bucket. Each product reserves three public slots per wow level (15 total), displayed 5-4-3-2-1 three times; surplus grounded findings remain reserve and weaker hypotheses remain developing.
high_order_inference.lifecycle_policy: Claim-native stock persists as page/reserve/developing tiers. Evidence is recomputed each scan; candidates can strengthen, weaken or move between tiers as new evidence arrives. Counter-evidence and falsifier results affect maturity and can kill a contradicted hypothesis, but an unrun challenge is not a ban on future-facing reasoning.
high_order_inference.candidate_search_policy: Missing-role and falsifier queries remain ordinary scanner discovery inputs and receive no admission waiver.

scenarios_2035.method: Two uncertainties define the frame: how many resources Europe has, and how strongly Europe is connected globally. The four worlds are scenarios, not forecasts. Each has four variants built from current shocks, risks and opportunities.

axes.horizontal: Less globally connected ↔ More globally connected

scenarios.name: Connected Growth
story: Europe enters 2035 with more money, capacity and research infrastructure, while staying strongly connected to global partners. Researchers, firms and universities can work across borders easily, and Europe scales more of what it discovers.
Trace it back and you find two of today's tugs of war settled one way: “The EU has adopted a framework for science diplomacy”; “Europe is investing more in AI”.
Not everything moved. “An older link between strategic investment finance and research-system governance is returning without being named.” That was true in the 2020s and it is true now.
Someone read the signs early: “Active capacity-building could expand AI-factory public procurement.” The bet worked.
The warning came early and was filed away: “Research collaboration is moving into practice before the rulebook catches up.” It is now the norm.
The trade-off is exposure: deeper global links also leave Europe more dependent on decisions, suppliers and disruptions outside Europe.

scenarios.name: Independent Scale
story: By 2035, strong European investment has built more research and technology capacity, but Europe works with a narrower set of global partners. Funding and infrastructure are strong, while security, resilience and European control shape who can take part.
It grew out of two arguments the 2020s never resolved, until they were: “Research security is expanding” and “New commitments strengthen venture capital”.
Some things never changed. In the 2020s the Radar noted: “Europe keeps returning to the same innovation-conversion problem.” In 2035 it still does.
One early bet paid off. The 2020s signal was “Strategic-autonomy goals could become the missing route into research-system governance.” In this world, it came true.
One risk quietly became routine: “A bottleneck in industrial competitiveness could propagate into strategic-autonomy goals.”
The trade-off is reach: Europe has more control, but fewer outside connections and less access to some global talent, markets and ideas.

scenarios.name: Open Under Pressure
story: Global links remain strong in 2035, but European research and innovation operate with tight resources. Ideas and people move easily, while many European teams depend on outside capital, infrastructure or partners to scale their work.
It is the world where today's evidence toward “Horizon access capacity is expanding” and “Constraints are slowing data centres” continues.
A familiar pattern survived the decade: “Research collaboration keeps changing shape, not disappearing.”
One door that looked half-open in the 2020s swung wide: “New funding could expand innovation regional capacity.”
And one warning was not heeded: “Horizon access is moving ahead of settled rules.” By 2035 it is simply how things work.
The trade-off is dependence: Europe stays connected, but often relies on others to finance, host or scale what it creates.

scenarios.name: Constrained Europe
story: In 2035, Europe has fewer resources and weaker global connections. Governments and institutions protect a smaller core of capabilities, while new projects, partnerships and large investments become harder to sustain.
Two pulls visible today carried it here: “Quantum governance is expanding”, and “Conditions around regional capacity are tightening”.
Old habits held. Back then the Radar kept seeing “Strategic autonomy keeps spreading through research and technology policy.” It never went away.
The lucky break was visible years ahead: “Active agreements could widen European drone capability.”
Nobody acted on this 2020s red flag: “Defence-innovation funding is moving into practice before the rulebook catches up.” Now everyone lives with it.
The trade-off is ambition: Europe reduces exposure, but has less capacity to build, experiment and compete at scale.

historical_context.reader_more: Researchers at the Technical University of Munich applied interrupted time-series analysis, which compares trends before and after an event, to data from April 2019 to April 2025. deep_analysis.work_kind: Quasi-experimental empirical study (interrupted time-series); journal article labelled 'Review'
deep_analysis.research_question: How did the April 2021 announcement of the EU AI Act influence market access and the pace of innovation for AI-enabled medical devices and healthcare products in the EU?
deep_analysis.main_finding: No sustained, statistically significant post-announcement change in EU-origin FDA approvals, Health AI Register device counts or WIPO AI patent filings; EU-origin FDA approvals showed a one-off level increase (beta2 about 2.0, p = 0.014) without a trend change. OECD/Preqin venture data showed larger descriptive increases for the EU27 (deals +117%, volume +146%) than other regions, with too few observations for inference.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Interrupted time-series analysis (OLS with Newey-West errors, 24-month lag) on monthly data April 2019–April 2025 from the FDA AI-enabled device list (121 devices from 14 EU countries), the Health AI Register and WIPO PATENTSCOPE; exploratory comparison (Welch's t-test) of annual OECD AI Policy Observatory venture data 2018–2024.
deep_analysis.qualification: Tests association with the Act's announcement, not its later implementation; proxies (FDA approvals of EU-made devices, registry counts, patents) are indirect, confounders such as COVID-19 are acknowledged, and the venture-capital comparison is descriptive only.

historical_context.reader_more: KU Leuven researchers used large-scale text analysis and supervised classification to sort project descriptions and resulting publications by research level, from basic biomedical science to patient-, population- and health-system-oriented work. They compared EU Framework Programme collaborative health research (FP7 and Horizon 2020) and European Research Council life-science grants with US National Institutes of Health collaborative programmes. The EU collaborative projects shifted markedly, while ERC grants and NIH's P01 and U01 programmes stayed more stable and dominated by basic research. Basic biomedical research remained central in publications even from EU collaborative projects. The authors conclude that funders' expectations change more than realised research trajectories.

At publication level changes were more moderate, with basic biomedical research remaining central even in FP-HR outputs, a partial translation of funding priorities.

historical_context.reader_more: The Value from Nordic Health Data project, funded by the Nordic Council of Ministers, has released a preliminary model for sharing and reusing health data across Nordic borders. The region has unusual advantages: comprehensive population registries, personal identification numbers that allow record linkage, high public trust and a shared emphasis on data protection. These have been underused because regulations are fragmented, access timelines long and GDPR interpreted differently between countries. The model rests on three connected areas, knowledge sharing about systems and structures, research collaboration and statistics, and a coordinating Driver function maintaining strategic alignment and ethical standards. It is framed around how the European Health Data Space will be implemented in the Nordics.

historical_context.reader_point: Abstract Thirty years after the dissolution of the USSR, the significant disparity between the research infrastructures of former Soviet republics and Western countries remains evident.

historical_context.reader_what: Only 28.3% of Armenian scholars published a Web of Science article in 2017–2021, versus over 98% of Italian academics.
historical_context.reader_why: Field-level strengths and gaps give Armenian policymakers evidence for reforms aimed at closer integration with the European Research Area.
historical_context.reader_more: Italian and Armenian researchers first review Armenia's post-Soviet reforms, including a new Higher Education and Science Committee, plans to move research institutes into universities, and publication thresholds for basic funding from 2026. They then apply Fractional Scientific Strength, a field-normalised productivity indicator developed by the Italian co-authors, to 2017–2021 Web of Science data for almost 4,000 Armenian scientists. Armenia lags Italy overall and has a much weaker presence in high-impact journals, though a few fields, such as integrative medicine and energy and fuels, come closer. The analysis relies on indexed journal output only.

deep_analysis.research_question: How does the research performance of Armenian scientists compare with Italian benchmarks after reforms intended to integrate Armenia's science system with the European Research Area?
deep_analysis.main_finding: Armenia lags Italy in research productivity and impact: only 28.3% of Armenian scholars published at least one WoS-indexed article in 2017–2021 versus over 98% of Italian academics, with a much weaker presence in high-impact journals; relative performance varies by field, with some (e.g. integrative and complementary medicine, energy and fuels) closer to Italian levels.
deep_analysis.method_or_basis: Review of Armenian science and higher-education reforms, then Fractional Scientific Strength (FSS) productivity measurement of almost 4,000 Armenian scientists on 2017–2021 Web of Science data, aggregated to field, institution and national level and benchmarked against Italian academics.
deep_analysis.qualification: Bibliometric indicators capture only Web of Science-indexed journal output; Italy is a single benchmark country; findings describe 2017–2021 performance, not the effects of the latest reforms.
deep_analysis.radar_relevance: Evidence on research-system convergence at the edge of the ERA: how a post-Soviet partner country's reforms toward European standards translate, or not, into research performance relative to an EU member state.

historical_context.reader_more: The Choose France CNRS AI Rising Talents programme, running since 2020, offers young researchers in France and abroad the chance to lead a four-year AI research project in a CNRS laboratory. The fourth annual call introduced two changes: it opened to French researchers with international backgrounds, aiming to attract and retain them, and it accepted projects at the interface with other disciplines rather than only core AI topics such as machine learning. historical_context.reader_more: The authors examine why EU Framework Programme funding is distributed so unevenly, moving below the country level to NUTS-2 regions and separating the higher education and private sectors. They analyse EUR 71.6 billion distributed between 2007 and 2020, measuring grant funding per unit of R&D personnel and testing how regional research personnel, R&D investment, research intensity and development level affect it, mediated by the amount of funding requested. In the private sector several southern European regions perform strongly, largely by applying for a great deal. In higher education the advantage lies with the blue banana regions, driven by high R&D investment and research intensity. From FP7 to Horizon 2020 private-sector divergence increased in favour of peripheral regions.

historical_context.reader_more: The authors ask whether there is a legal foundation for responsible research assessment and what obstacles stand in the way of turning reform into practice. They analyse sources ranging from binding hard law through soft law to self-regulation, at EU level and in Italy as a national case. They find that apart from constitutional and legal provisions on freedom of research, university autonomy, non-discrimination and gender equality, the foundation rests mainly on soft law and policy norms such as Council conclusions and the 2022 Agreement on Reforming Research Assessment, which is explicitly not legally binding. They conclude self-regulation is the most promising route at this stage.

It designates materials as strategic based on relevance and expected demand, and sets benchmarks for minimum shares of EU demand met by domestic extraction, processing and recycling, while aiming to reduce dependence on single third-country suppliers at every supply chain step. historical_context.reader_why: Whoever shapes technical standards shapes which technologies and industries can compete.
historical_context.reader_more: Technology standards were long set mainly by companies and technical experts, but great power competition has pushed Western states toward greater intervention, including an EU-US mechanism for coordinating on what they call common strategic issues. Meanwhile China has expanded its presence in standards development organisations, secured more technical leadership positions, and uses the Belt and Road Initiative to promote its standards in partner countries. The authors explain why this matters: standards enable interoperability, economies of scale and trade, and those who shape them are well placed to shape entire industries. Their recommendation is that Europeans avoid escalating the standards arena into open confrontation with China while remaining watchful and building their own capacity to participate effectively.

historical_context.reader_more: The author asks how European integration extends into outer space, taking the Ariane launcher as her case. Jointly built by thirteen countries and heavily subsidised, Ariane has been treated as a symbol of European technological integration since the European Space Agency's founding objective of building a European launcher. Controversies about its future entangle questions of innovation, security and geopolitical power, especially as commercial competitors reshape the sector. Using the concept of sociotechnical imaginaries from science and technology studies, and drawing on two years of fieldwork including interviews and participant observation in the European space sector plus document analysis of space policy reports, she traces which space futures are projected onto Ariane and how they relate to the ideals and tensions of European integration.

historical_context.reader_more: Most people never take part in a formal climate policy consultation, but many play video games. The EU-funded GREAT project, coordinated from Germany's Leibniz Institute for Research and Information in Education, tested whether games could open a channel between citizens and policymakers. Working with PlanetPlay and more than 30 studios, it embedded short climate surveys inside popular mobile titles, reaching around 130 million players, with 1.2 million engaging and over 200,000 completing them. The project also ran collaborative dilemma games in Austria, Cyprus and the United Kingdom to generate deeper qualitative discussion. The researchers are candid that large-scale engagement is only half the problem: turning input into policy would need much closer involvement from policymakers.

historical_context.reader_more: In 2015 NordForsk launched a Nordic Centres of Excellence call on the role of water in the bioeconomy, preceded by multi-level negotiations between Nordic countries; all participated except Denmark, with a total call budget of NOK 90 million. The centres were funded for five years between 2017 and 2022, with NordForsk joined as funders by the research councils of Norway, Finland and Sweden and Iceland's Rannis. Looking back, the account reports that the added value lay in broad researcher networking and cooperation forums, that expansion of research capacity was crucial and well delivered, and that research quality rose, reflected in a large number of scientific articles. Competence developed in aquaculture, fisheries, hydrological modelling and ecosystem services, with a strong interdisciplinary approach across all centres.

historical_context.reader_title: What the Ukraine war revealed about space as a security domain
historical_context.reader_what: Commercial satellite services proved decisive, blurring military and civilian lines and pushing states toward sovereign space capability.
historical_context.reader_why: Reliance on commercial space assets reshapes what European space capability must provide.
historical_context.reader_more: This Hybrid CoE working paper examines how the space domain has been used and affected during the war in Ukraine, which the authors argue has been used more versatilely than in any previous conflict. Crowdsourced situational awareness from civilians has supported field operations, while satellite-based technologies have become everyday tools for military and civilian users alike, showing that access to space capabilities matters more than owning them. That reliance on commercial assets in military operations blurs the line between military and civilian actors, and advances in satellite technology enable new capability combinations. A major consequence has been the degradation of cooperative spirit in international space programmes, pushing countries toward national and regional activity to secure sovereignty.

historical_context.reader_what: Collaboration matters more than R&D for SME innovation, and its effect varies strongly by regional context.
historical_context.reader_why: Implies EU innovation policy built on a uniform R&D-intensity target misallocates effort in weaker regions.
historical_context.reader_more: EU innovation policy has long been organised around raising R&D investment towards three per cent of GDP. The authors argue this is place-blind, because SME innovation draws on internal R&D, non-R&D inputs and external collaboration, all shaped by location. Using Regional Innovation Scoreboard data covering 220 regions in 22 European countries, they find SMEs in more innovative regions benefit from combining internal R&D, collaboration of all kinds and non-R&D inputs, while SMEs in less innovative regions depend mainly on external sources and especially on collaboration with other firms. Greater public R&D investment does not reliably improve regional SME innovation. They conclude that a more collaboration-based, place-sensitive policy is needed.

historical_context.reader_why: Mobility requirements built on a binary view can penalise researchers whose constraints are structural and gendered.
historical_context.reader_more: Swiss academia has the highest inbound and outbound mobility in Europe and, in line with European Research Area aims, funds scientific mobility and extended research stays as tools for collaboration and excellence. Institutions have simultaneously worried that female academics are less mobile and that local family ties damage their careers. historical_context.reader_title: OECD report on precarious postdoctoral careers and how to reduce them
historical_context.reader_what: Precarity among postdoctoral researchers is widespread across OECD systems, worsened but not caused by Covid-19.
historical_context.reader_why: Prolonged precarity narrows who can stay in research, affecting talent retention and the quality of science.
historical_context.reader_more: The report focuses on the research precariat, defined as postdoctoral researchers on fixed-term positions without permanent or continuous employment prospects. It finds precarity widespread across OECD countries and research systems, with Covid-19 aggravating a pre-existing problem rather than creating it. Doctorate attainment rose about twenty-five per cent across the OECD between 2014 and 2019 while secure academic positions did not keep pace, producing long postdoctoral periods on short-term contracts. It reports detrimental effects on wellbeing, opaque selection procedures, concerns about workforce diversity, and women disproportionately leaving at the early-to-mid career transition. It argues a publish-or-perish culture imperils research quality. It offers nine recommendations spanning working conditions, professional development, equal opportunities, funding and human resource links, mobility, evidence and governance.

historical_context.reader_more: The chapter defines EU digital sovereignty as the capacity to influence information technology norms and standards in order to preserve the internal market's integrity, foundational EU values, and the ability to act independently in geopolitical competition over the digital sphere. It notes that digital sovereignty was a top priority for the Commission's mandate. The author examines three fields, digital economy, data protection and artificial intelligence, assuming the EU's normative and economic weight gives it the best prospects there. On artificial intelligence it identifies a further ambition: competing strategically with China and the United States through a values-based third path.

historical_context.reader_more: The authors note that the Commission's Horizon Europe proposal was the first EU framework programme proposal prepared using a major foresight exercise, the BOHEMIA project, which brought the Sustainable Development Goals into the preparation debate. Drawing on transition management, they argue that success in pursuing the goals depends on the reflexivity of governance, and that foresight is how reflexivity is built in. Whether the Commission delivers that, they leave open.

historical_context.reader_more: Concentration in research funding has long been contested, defended as a way to focus investment and criticised as a route to hypercompetition, reduced diversity and conservative topic choice. Most previous studies looked at concentration within single funding organisations. The authors instead take a systemic view, examining nearly twenty thousand competitive grants allocated by fifteen major Danish research funders. They find allocation strongly skewed towards a small elite of individual researchers and towards a selected group of research areas and topics. historical_context.reader_more: The article explains a term that entered Dutch research and innovation debate: mission-driven innovation policy. In July 2018 the responsible ministers set out innovation policy focused on four major societal themes: energy transition and sustainability; agriculture, water and food; health and care; and safety. The piece argues this is a logical step in the history of innovation policy and traces the inspiration to earlier missions such as the Delta Works and the Apollo programme, while noting an important difference: those missions were mainly technically complicated, whereas current themes are far more complex and therefore need a different kind of mission. It describes the 2019 elaboration requiring many parties to work together on each theme, extending beyond knowledge institutions, companies, research funders and ministries.

The authors argue these policies can seriously alter classic innovation dynamics. In offshore wind, a specific institutional architecture produced a dominant design very early in the technology's development, with radical experimentation only beginning to appear after twenty years of diffusion, reversing the usual pathway. They conclude that rapid dominant design and diffusion help countries meet climate pledges but risk early lock-in.

historical_context.reader_more: Some European politicians have held up Chinese industrial policy, and firms such as CRRC and Huawei, as examples to follow. The author argues this ignores the downsides of an approach that works only under China's hybrid state capitalism, where market forces are welcome only when they serve strategic goals. Market distortions, duplicated local initiatives, overcapacity and rising debt are tolerated because the party controls everything, at the cost of entrepreneurial vitality. European conditions differ: priorities are set democratically, firms are autonomous and social market values hold. The piece assesses the Commission's March 2020 industrial strategy as moving in the right direction, noting its focus on SMEs, its call for trial-and-error research and pan-European industrial alliances, and warns its assumptions of EU high-tech leadership need unbiased assessment.

historical_context.reader_title: How Europe, India and China build ethics into science and innovation policy
historical_context.reader_what: Europe institutionalises ethics mainly through advisory and deliberative bodies protecting rights; India and China steer STI toward development goals.
historical_context.reader_why: Explains the distinctive European model of ethics governance underpinning responsible research and innovation.
historical_context.reader_more: The authors distinguish ethical governance (compliance), ethical deliberation (advisory debate) and ethical reflection. In Europe, national ethics councils, the European Group on Ethics and technology assessment bodies combine expert and lay input and act as early warning systems. India frames STI ethics around inclusion, access and equity. China emphasises research integrity and harnessing science for national development. The comparison shows the European approach is not universal.

historical_context.reader_title: European academies set out what digital humanities research needs
historical_context.reader_what: ALLEA recommends open humanities data, sustained research infrastructures, new publishing models and career recognition for digital skills.
historical_context.reader_why: Frames European research-infrastructure and open-science choices for humanities as digitisation transformed scholarship.
historical_context.reader_more: The E-Humanities Working Group of All European Academies describes how digitisation, encoding, data analysis and linked data change humanities research. It identifies enablers: responsible open access to data, durable and interoperable infrastructures, trusted digital archives, and recognition of data work in careers. It points to DARIAH, the Research Data Alliance and Horizon 2020 research-data policy. It also reports on a 2013 survey of academies’ digital projects.

historical_context.reader_title: Using the EU’s ERIC instrument to govern pan-European biobank research
historical_context.reader_what: Chapter examines the European Research Infrastructure Consortium as an EU governance tool, focusing on biobanking infrastructure BBMRI.
historical_context.reader_more: The chapter studies the European Research Infrastructure Consortium (ERIC), a legal form created by the EU for jointly run research infrastructures. Its case is BBMRI, the pan-European biobanking infrastructure financed by the EU and participating states. The notes show the analysis engages EU constitutional law and the fragmented national rules on consent and ethics review for biobank research. The research was done within the Swedish BBMRI node.
